OIIX.name: FIR Tehran
OIIX.conflictType: Interstate conflict — Iran vs Israel/US (fragile ceasefire)
OIIX.narrative: EASA's CZIB-2026-04 reflects a ceasefire that has held since April 2026 but remains fragile, with an elevated Iranian air-defence posture that raises the risk of civil aircraft being misidentified. EASA has warned escalation could resume with little notice. The eastern part of the FIR was partially reopened for overflights in June 2026, while the western part remains closed; most Europe-Asia traffic continues to route south via Egypt/Saudi or north via the Caucasus/Afghanistan. Iran has previously conducted missile activity close to busy international routes with little warning to civil aviation, and the shoot-down of Ukraine International Airlines flight 752 over Tehran in Jan 2020 illustrates how quickly the situation can deteriorate.

cross.detail: July 2026: Renewed military action and attacks around the Strait of Hormuz have effectively broken down the US-Iran ceasefire. EASA's current CZIB continues to advise against operating in the OIIX/Tehran FIR at any altitude. The primary risk remains misidentification of civil aircraft by air-defence systems during periods of heightened tension. Several states continue to warn against operations in Iranian airspace. Major events: June 2026: Eastern OIIX/Tehran FIR partially reopened; western part remains closed. March 2026: OIIX/Tehran FIR closed following large-scale US and Israeli strikes on Iranian military targets and subsequent Iranian missile and drone retaliation. June 2025: Israel and Iran exchanged missile strikes, prompting renewed airspace warnings. Oct 2024: Israel and Iran carried out missile attacks against each other, leading most international operators to avoid both airspaces. Jan 2020: Iran shot down Ukraine International Airlines flight 752 over Tehran after misidentifying the aircraft as a hostile target.

ORBB.name: FIR Baghdad
ORBB.conflictType: Non-state armed groups (IBMGs) + Iranian missile/drone spillover
ORBB.narrative: Despite the regional ceasefire, EASA cites recurrent Iranian drone and ballistic-missile strikes reaching Iraqi airspace, alongside the continued presence of Iranian-backed militant groups (IBMGs), as reasons the Baghdad FIR remains a do-not-operate zone. Iraqi airspace reopened to overflights in June 2026 following the US-Iran ceasefire, with north-south routes available, though most Europe-Asia traffic still routes south via Egypt/Saudi or north via the Caucasus/Afghanistan. Additional risks include potential misidentification by air-defence systems operated by local and foreign military forces, and an ongoing threat from terrorist groups with portable anti-aircraft weaponry.

cross.detail: July 2026: Renewed military action and attacks around the Strait of Hormuz have effectively broken down the US-Iran ceasefire. Despite that, Iraqi airspace (the ORBB/Baghdad FIR) remains open to overflights and some operators continue using it. EASA's current CZIB continues to advise against operating in the ORBB/Baghdad FIR at any altitude. Several states continue to maintain airspace warnings for Iraq. Major events: June 2026: ORBB/Baghdad FIR reopened to overflights following the US-Iran ceasefire. March 2026: ORBB/Baghdad FIR closed following US and Israeli strikes on Iran and subsequent Iranian retaliation. June 2025: Airspace closed following Israeli missile attack on Iran; missiles and drones transited Iraqi airspace. Apr 2024: Airspace closed due to Iranian drone and missile strike on Israel. Apr 2023: Several drone and missile attacks in northern Iraq launched from Turkey and Iran, including strikes near ORSU and ORER. Oct 2021: US operators permitted to overfly the ORBB/Baghdad FIR above FL320 under updated FAA restrictions.

OLBB.name: FIR Beirut
OLBB.narrative: A Trilateral Framework Agreement between Israel, Lebanon and the US (26 June 2026) is a step toward consolidating the ceasefire, but EASA notes its long-term implementation is uncertain, and that Lebanon has not shown it can proactively manage airspace risk. Israeli airstrikes in Lebanon continue, and most international operators avoid the airspace. Some states allow limited operations to OLBA/Beirut provided arrivals and departures remain over the Mediterranean Sea. GNSS spoofing and jamming have also been reported in the OLBB/Beirut FIR from November 2023 onwards.

cross.detail: July 2026: Renewed military action and attacks around the Strait of Hormuz have effectively broken down the US-Iran ceasefire. Israeli airstrikes in Lebanon continue. EASA's current CZIB continues to advise against operating in the OLBB/Beirut FIR at any altitude. Several states maintain long-standing warnings advising operators to avoid Lebanese airspace. Major events: Feb-Jul 2026: Israeli airstrikes continued in Lebanon despite repeated ceasefire extensions and diplomatic efforts. Oct 2024: Israel launched a ground operation against Hezbollah in southern Lebanon. Nov 2023 - ongoing: GNSS spoofing and jamming reported in the OLBB/Beirut FIR.

OJAC.name: FIR Amman
OJAC.conflictType: Missile/drone overflight risk (regional spillover, no direct conflict on Jordanian soil)
OJAC.narrative: Jordan's airspace has repeatedly seen Iranian missiles and drones pass through en route to other targets, intercepted by Jordanian and allied air defences. Jordanian authorities have not published any airspace restrictions of their own despite this activity. Jordan remained open throughout the Iran conflict, though missile and drone activity affected several neighbouring countries. EASA has issued an Information Note advising operators to take the potential risk into account before operating in the OJAC/Amman FIR.

cross.detail: July 2026: Renewed military action and attacks around the Strait of Hormuz have effectively broken down the US-Iran ceasefire. Jordan airspace (the OJAC/Amman FIR) remains open and operating normally. EASA's current Information Note advises operators to take the potential risk into account before operating in the OJAC/Amman FIR. Major events: July 2026: EASA issued a new Information Note for the OJAC/Amman FIR following renewed military activity in the Gulf. Feb-Jul 2026: Jordan remained open throughout the Iran conflict, although missile and drone activity affected several neighbouring countries. Apr 2024: Jordan temporarily closed its airspace during the Iranian drone and missile attack on Israel. Oct 2023: Jordan intercepted drones and missiles transiting its airspace during regional escalation.

OKAC.name: FIR Kuwait
OKAC.conflictType: Interstate tension — Iran vs US (Strait of Hormuz)
OKAC.narrative: Kuwait hosts major US military facilities, making it a plausible target for Iranian retaliation and increasing the risk of civil aircraft being caught up in an attack or an air-defence response. Kuwait has been directly affected by strikes, including missile and drone damage to OKKK/Kuwait airport in March 2026. The FIR is currently open for arrivals and departures only; overflights remain prohibited.

cross.detail: July 2026: Renewed military action and attacks around the Strait of Hormuz have effectively broken down the US-Iran ceasefire. The OKAC/Kuwait FIR remains open for arrivals and departures only — overflights continue to be prohibited. EASA's current CZIB advises against operating in the OKAC/Kuwait FIR at any altitude. Major events: July 2026: EASA issued a new CZIB for the OKAC/Kuwait FIR following renewed military activity in the Gulf. Feb-Jul 2026: OKAC/Kuwait FIR closed and reopened several times during the Iran conflict. March 2026: Missile and drone strikes damaged OKKK/Kuwait airport. June 2025: Israel and Iran exchanged missile strikes across the region.

OBBB.name: FIR Bahrain
OBBB.conflictType: Interstate tension — Iran vs US (Strait of Hormuz)
OBBB.narrative: As with Kuwait and Qatar, the US military presence in Bahrain is the main driver of EASA's risk assessment for this FIR. Bahrain lies close to several key military facilities in the Gulf region. The FIR closed and reopened several times during the Iran conflict before returning to normal overflight operations, but EASA's CZIB now advises against operating at any altitude.

cross.detail: July 2026: Renewed military action and attacks around the Strait of Hormuz have effectively broken down the US-Iran ceasefire. Bahrain airspace (the OBBB/Bahrain FIR) remains open to overflights. EASA's current CZIB advises against operating in the OBBB/Bahrain FIR at any altitude. Major events: July 2026: EASA issued a new CZIB for the OBBB/Bahrain FIR following renewed military activity in the Gulf. Feb-Jul 2026: OBBB/Bahrain FIR closed and reopened several times during the Iran conflict before reopening to normal overflight operations. March 2026: Iranian missile and drone attacks targeted several Gulf states, including incidents affecting airspace around Bahrain. June 2025: Israel and Iran exchanged missile strikes, prompting renewed airspace warnings across the region.

OTDF.name: FIR Doha
OTDF.conflictType: Interstate tension — Iran vs US (Strait of Hormuz)
OTDF.narrative: Qatar hosts significant US forces and has itself been targeted by Iranian strikes during the recent escalation — including a missile strike reported at Al Udeid Air Base near Doha in March 2026 — keeping it on EASA's do-not-operate list even as operational conditions ease. The FIR is currently open and operating largely normally.

cross.detail: July 2026: Renewed military action and attacks around the Strait of Hormuz have effectively broken down the US-Iran ceasefire. Qatar airspace (the OTDF/Doha FIR) remains open and operating largely normally. EASA's current CZIB advises against operating in the OTDF/Doha FIR at any altitude. Major events: July 2026: EASA issued a new CZIB for the OTDF/Doha FIR following renewed military activity in the Gulf. Feb-Jul 2026: OTDF/Doha FIR closed and reopened several times during the Iran conflict before reopening to normal overflight operations. March 2026: Iranian missile strike reported at Al Udeid Air Base near Doha. June 2025: Israel and Iran exchanged missile strikes, prompting renewed airspace warnings across the region.

OMAE.name: FIR Emirates
OMAE.conflictType: Interstate tension — Iran vs US (Strait of Hormuz)
OMAE.narrative: The UAE's proximity to the Strait of Hormuz and its role as a regional hub keep it firmly within EASA's risk assessment, despite being operationally busy.

OOMM.name: FIR Muscat — west of 58°E only
OOMM.conflictType: Interstate tension — Iran vs US (Strait of Hormuz)
OOMM.narrative: Unlike other Gulf FIRs, only the western portion of Omani/Gulf of Oman waters is covered — reflecting where commercial vessel attacks and Strait of Hormuz tension actually concentrate. Oman itself remained open throughout the Iran conflict and became a key part of the main southern bypass route (Egypt-Saudi-Oman) used by many operators.

cross.detail: July 2026: Renewed military action and attacks around the Strait of Hormuz have effectively broken down the US-Iran ceasefire. Oman airspace (the OOMM/Muscat FIR) remains open and is a key part of the main southern bypass route, carrying significant Europe-Asia overflight traffic. EASA's current CZIB advises against operating over the waters of the Gulf of Oman within the OOMM/Muscat FIR west of 58°E. The primary risk is spillover of missile or drone activity from conflicts elsewhere in the region. Major events: July 2026: EASA issued a new CZIB advising operators not to operate over the waters of the Gulf of Oman within the OOMM/Muscat FIR west of 58°E. Feb-Jul 2026: Oman remained open throughout the Iran conflict and became a key part of the main southern bypass route. June 2025: Israel and Iran exchanged missile strikes, prompting renewed airspace warnings across the Gulf region. Oct 2024: Israel and Iran carried out missile attacks against each other, leading many operators to avoid airspace between the two countries.

OSTT.name: FIR Damascus
OSTT.narrative: EASA's longest-running Middle East bulletin (19 revisions since 2017) reflects a still-unresolved multi-actor conflict. Traffic patterns have shifted: OSTT quietly reopened to some regional carriers in early 2025 as an alternative to the more restricted Iran/Iraq corridor, even though most Western operators continue to avoid it. Risks include Israeli airstrikes targeting Iranian and Hezbollah-linked positions and potential misidentification by air-defence systems.

cross.detail: July 2026: Renewed military action and attacks around the Strait of Hormuz have effectively broken down the US-Iran ceasefire. Syrian airspace (the OSTT/Damascus FIR) remains high risk, but some regional operators have started using it as an alternative to the more restricted Iran/Iraq routing. Several countries continue to prohibit or advise against operations in the OSTT/Damascus FIR due to military operations, anti-aviation weaponry and unstable security conditions. Major events: March 2026: OSTT/Damascus FIR closed following US and Israeli strikes on Iran and subsequent Iranian retaliation. Jan-Jul 2026: Gradual increase in overflights through Syria as some regional operators use the FIR as an alternative to Iran and Iraq. Dec 2024: Syrian airspace temporarily closed following the fall of the Assad regime. Oct 2023: Airstrikes damaged runways at OSDI/Damascus and OSAP/Aleppo airports. Feb 2020: An A320 approaching Damascus diverted after being caught in crossfire during Israeli airstrikes. Sep 2018: Russian IL-20 shot down in error near the Syria-Cyprus FIR boundary.

OYSC.name: FIR Sana'a only
OYSC.conflictType: Civil war + interstate spillover (Red Sea attacks)
OYSC.narrative: This bulletin covers only the Sana'a FIR, not the whole of Yemen. The ongoing civil war and Houthi involvement in the wider regional conflict keep the risk assessment unchanged since 2017.

cross.detail: Yemen remains an active conflict zone; the vast majority of Yemeni airspace (OYSC/Sanaa FIR) should be avoided. Several countries prohibit aircraft from overflying any land portion of the FIR. US operators can still use offshore routes UT702 and M999, while other countries permit flights on overwater portions of Yemeni airspace. Saudi airspace to the north and Somali airspace to the south also carry risks. The primary risk is intentional targeting by terrorist groups with access to sophisticated anti-aircraft weaponry. Civil aircraft are also at risk from high-intensity military operations including explosive drones and missiles. Saudi and Israeli airstrikes can occur at any time, including in the capital Sana'a. Major events: Jul 2026: Yemen's government carried out an airstrike on the runway at OYSN/Sanaa Airport to stop an Iranian aircraft from landing. Dec 2024 - ongoing: OYSN/Sanaa Airport closed due to damage from Israeli airstrikes in Dec 2024 and May 2025. Jan 2024: US and UK carried out airstrikes against Houthi rebels in Yemen in response to missile and drone attacks in the Red Sea. Sep 2023: Houthi drone attacks near the Yemen-Saudi border. Apr-Oct 2022: All parties in the Yemeni conflict agreed a ceasefire. 2018-2022: Frequent Saudi airstrikes on Sanaa and other targets in Yemen in retaliation for Houthi drone attacks. 2017: OYSN/Sanaa Airport badly damaged by coalition airstrikes.

UUWV.name: FIR Moscow and others (west of 60°E)
UUWV.conflictType: Interstate war — Russian invasion of Ukraine (air-defence risk)
UUWV.narrative: Issued after the likely accidental shoot-down of Azerbaijan Airlines flight 8243 near Grozny in December 2024, this bulletin reflects the risk that Russian air-defence systems responding to Ukrainian strikes pose to civil aircraft, compounded by widespread GNSS interference. Drone attacks across Russia have been escalating, with some reaching as far as Siberia; Russian air-defence systems use surface-to-air missiles capable of reaching all altitudes, so the risk applies at every level. Ukraine's airspace has remained fully closed to civil aviation since the Russian invasion in Feb 2022, and several countries prohibit their operators from using Russian airspace near the FIR boundaries with Ukraine.

cross.detail: As of June 2025, drone attacks across Russia are ramping up, with some reaching as far as Siberia, increasing the risk for any aircraft still using Russian airspace. Hundreds of drones have been shot down recently, including in areas around Moscow. While most operators avoid Russian airspace completely, those still flying there should be prepared for sudden closures or reroutes. Most activity happens at night, but daytime disruptions are now common too. The primary risk is unintended targeting of civil aircraft by military systems near the Russia-Ukraine border, including misidentification. Major events: Jan 2025: EASA issued a new CZIB recommending against flights in western Russia (anywhere west of 60°E) due to the threat of anti-aircraft fire and high danger of misidentification by air-defence systems targeting Ukrainian drones and missiles. This follows the shoot-down of a passenger jet at URMG/Grozny on Dec 25. Jan 2024: Crash of a military transport aircraft in Russian airspace near Belgorod, approx 20nm from the Ukrainian border. Both Russia and Ukraine accused each other of shooting it down. Aug 2023: Private jet carrying Wagner mercenary chief Yevgeny Prigozhin crashed en route from Moscow to St Petersburg on Aug 23. July 2023 - ongoing: Several incidents of drone strikes on targets in Moscow and surrounding region, with some drones damaging buildings and Moscow airports forced to close temporarily on many occasions.

UKBV.name: All Ukrainian FIRs
UKBV.narrative: In force since the day of the invasion, this remains one of the clearest and most stable prohibitions in this dataset — Ukraine itself has closed its FIRs to civil traffic by NOTAM. All major countries that regularly issue airspace warnings (the US, UK, Canada, France, Germany, Italy) have issued total flight bans for Ukraine due to risk from military activity at all levels.

cross.detail: Ukraine closed its entire airspace to all civil traffic on Feb 24, 2022, due to a military invasion by Russia. Russia, Belarus and Moldova have closed large sections of their own airspace near to their FIR boundaries with Ukraine. The primary risk is unintended targeting of civil aircraft by military, including misidentification (as with MAS17, UIA752). The secondary risk is potential loss of Ukrainian ATC service at short notice (e.g. cyber attack) and other unforeseeable non-normal operating environments. Prior to February 2022, there were two areas of concern in Ukraine: the conflict in the far east (affecting UKDV/Dnipro FIR) and the disputed ATC authority over Crimea (UKFV/URFV/Simferopol FIR).

HSSS.name: FIR Khartoum
HSSS.conflictType: Civil war — Sudan Armed Forces (SAF) vs Rapid Support Forces (RSF)
HSSS.narrative: The ongoing SAF–RSF civil war has put anti-aircraft artillery, MANPADS and SAM systems into play across the whole of Sudanese airspace, keeping the entire Khartoum FIR off-limits. HSSK/Khartoum airport is closed but NOTAMs are not being issued; a Contingency Plan with published overflight routes via HSPN/Port Sudan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and South Sudan is available. The primary risk on the ground for any unplanned diversion is the security situation, with passenger jets having been targeted by gunfire at HSSK/Khartoum Airport. South Sudan's airspace also carries risk due to poor ATC provision below FL245.

cross.detail: Following a military coup in April 2023, Sudan remains closed to all civilian flights. In South Sudan, air navigation services remain suspended above FL245. There is ongoing fighting between government and militant forces. HSSK/Khartoum airport is closed, but no NOTAMs are being issued. A Contingency Plan with published overflight routes via HSPN/Port Sudan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and South Sudan is available. Several countries advise operators not to enter Sudanese airspace due to risks from anti-aircraft weaponry and military activity. Major events: Nov 2025: Il-76 reportedly shot down by a surface-to-air missile near Babanusa, southern Sudan. May 2025: Drone attack targeting critical infrastructure including HSPN/Port Sudan airport. Oct 2024: Foreign-registered cargo aircraft shot down by local militia over North Darfur, near the border with Chad. Apr 2023: Military coup on Apr 15; Sudan's airspace closed, South Sudan's airspace closed above FL245. Oct 2021: Military coup on Oct 25; HSSK/Khartoum airport closed for two days with all flights suspended.

HLLL.name: FIR Tripoli
HLLL.narrative: Libya's two rival governments and various non-state armed actors create a real risk of misidentification when crossing between areas controlled by different authorities. The one carve-out is for coastal airport approaches made from over the sea. Reliable ATC services cannot be guaranteed, with regular ATS and radar outages and severe VHF limitations; operators have at times had to communicate with Malta ATC for guidance.
HLLL.restrictionLabel: Do not operate, except flights to coastal airports approached from the sea, subject to ATC contact and your own risk assessment

cross.detail: A civil war has been ongoing since 2014. Libyan airspace (HLLL/Tripoli FIR) should be avoided entirely. A total flight ban applies for US operators; several other countries have warnings in place. The primary risk is misidentification by Libyan air-defence systems or by militia who have threatened to shoot down aircraft operating in western Libya, including at HLLM/Tripoli Mitiga airport. Military activity has been reported over the high seas, either operating as OAT or without ATC contact. Risk remains high at all flight levels. Major events: August 2023: Major evacuation of aircraft from Tripoli due to violent clashes and gunfire at Mitiga airport. July 2023: Italy cancelled its 10-year ban on flights to/from Libya. Aug 2022: Militia air-defence forces claimed to have shot down a US drone near Benghazi during increased tensions between competing militias. June 2022: Failed militia attempt to seize control of government offices in Tripoli resulted in armed clashes and suspension of flights at HLLM/Mitiga airport. Jan 2020: Multiple airstrikes targeting HLLM/Mitiga airport. Nov 2019: Militia declared a no-fly-zone around Tripoli, threatening to shoot down civil aircraft attempting to fly to HLLM/Mitiga airport. 2014: HLLT/Tripoli airport closed after rival militia clashes destroyed most facilities; most flights now operate from HLLM/Mitiga airport.

DRRR.name: Malian territory, especially the north-east
DRRR.conflictType: Insurgency — non-state armed groups active across the Sahel
DRRR.narrative: Non-state armed groups operating in Mali, particularly in the north-east, are assessed to have MANPADS and SAM missile capability, which is why the restriction is altitude-based rather than a total ban. ATS in Mali is provided by the GOOO/Dakar and DRRR/Niamey FIRs, which have a long-standing restriction for overflights of Mali to published ATS routes at FL320 and above. The security situation escalated sharply in April 2026, with coordinated nationwide attacks against state and military targets including gunfire and explosions near GABS/Bamako.

cross.detail: The conflict in northern and central Mali has continued since 2012 and the security situation remains volatile. Several countries have airspace warnings in place, typically advising operations at or above FL250 or FL260 and avoiding GATB/Timbuktu, GAGO/Gao and GAKL/Kidal. The US advises caution in Mali airspace at all levels due to ongoing fighting, expanding militant activity, and the presence of a state-run paramilitary force operating anti-aircraft systems, military aircraft, UAS and electronic warfare equipment. Primary risks include MANPADS and other surface-to-air weapons, indirect fire near airports, and potential misidentification or spillover from military activity. Low-level and airport-phase operations carry the highest exposure. Major events: April 2026: Multiple armed groups carried out coordinated attacks nationwide on Apr 25, with gunfire and explosions reported near GABS/Bamako; sporadic fighting is ongoing. France has issued a new airspace warning advising French operators not to operate to/from GABS or use it as an alternate. Sep 2024: Insurgents breached GABS/Bamako and set the presidential jet on fire; multiple attacks occurred across the city and the airport closed temporarily. Dec 2023: Germany prohibited its operators below FL260 in northern Mali; commercial flights to GATB/Timbuktu cancelled after shelling near the airport; a military jet crashed near GAGO/Gao with reports it may have been shot down. Aug 2020: All airports closed for two days during a military coup; Bamako ACC remained operational and overflights were unaffected. Apr 2018: Militants attacked UN bases near GATB/Timbuktu using indirect fire and vehicle bombs. Jan 2017 and Nov 2016: Vehicle bomb and rocket attacks targeted GAGO/Gao and GATB/Timbuktu airports.

HCSM.name: Somali airspace
HCSM.conflictType: Insurgency — Al-Shabaab and related terrorist groups
HCSM.narrative: Terrorist organisations operating in Somalia are assessed to have confirmed anti-aircraft weaponry, possibly including MANPADS, driving the same FL260 altitude floor as Mali. An additional risk arises from unauthorised ATC units issuing conflicting climb/descent instructions on official frequencies. From November 2025, Somaliland has claimed all overflights in the north of the FIR require a PPR from its own CAA, while Somalia maintains through an AIC that it controls the entire FIR — operators should expect conflicting permit instructions near Hargeisa and northern Somalia.

cross.detail: The situation on the ground is highly unstable. The central government has little control of major cities and ports, with ongoing attacks from extremist militants who continue to show intent to target aviation. The primary risk is to overflying aircraft at lower flight levels, which may be targeted by anti-aircraft-capable weapons. The US prohibits flights across Somalia's airspace (the HCSM/Mogadishu FIR) below FL260, except for flights transiting the overwater portion going to/from HDAM/Djibouti airport. Several other countries have issued warnings advising against operating below FL260. A secondary risk comes from unauthorised ATC units issuing conflicting instructions, and from the Somaliland authority dispute in the north of the FIR. Major events: Feb 2024: Several reports of aircraft within the Mogadishu FIR being contacted by a fake controller on the same frequency, issuing conflicting instructions. Aug 2023: Reports of uncontrolled operations including combat helicopters flying at FL030 without position or routing reports. Oct 2022: Somali government warned that HCMM/Mogadishu airport may be targeted by militant groups. May 2022: Class A airspace implemented in the HCSM/Mogadishu FIR above FL245. 2020-ongoing: Multiple Al-Shabaab attacks on HCMM/Mogadishu and nearby targets, including a UN compound. May 2020: An Embraer EMB-120 was shot down on approach to Bardale airstrip, killing all six people on board — an accidental shoot-down by Ethiopian forces combating Al-Shabaab.

OPKR.name: Baluchistan province (partial)
OPKR.conflictType: Insurgency (violent non-state actors) + Kashmir territorial dispute
OPKR.narrative: Violent non-state actor (VNSA) groups with confirmed MANPADS operate in Baluchistan. The Kashmir dispute separately raises misidentification risk further north. In May 2025 there were four days of intense cross-border shelling and aerial activity in Kashmir; a ceasefire announced on 10 May has largely held but the situation remains fragile. Current guidance generally advises operators to remain at or above FL260.

cross.detail: Tensions between Pakistan and India in the disputed Kashmir region, along with longstanding militant activity in parts of western Pakistan, create an ongoing risk in the OPKR/Karachi and OPLR/Lahore FIRs. Several states and EASA maintain altitude-based restrictions rather than full avoidance, generally advising operators to remain at or above FL260. The primary risks are from anti-aviation weaponry including the potential availability of MANPADS below FL260, and inadvertent risk from military activity or misidentification in the Kashmir region. Major events: Feb 2026: Cross-border strikes between Pakistan and Afghanistan escalated; no new airspace closures issued and commercial traffic continues to transit OAKX/Kabul FIR, including via P500 and G500. May 2025: Four days of cross-border strikes and shelling between India and Pakistan in the Kashmir region; ceasefire announced on 10 May has largely held. Some operators temporarily rerouted south via the Gulf of Oman and UAE. Jan 2024: Iran conducted missile and drone strikes against a militant group in western Pakistan, highlighting cross-border military activity risk. Dec 2023 - ongoing: Crew reports of GPS spoofing in the OPLR/Lahore FIR area, particularly around OPLA/Lahore. Feb-Aug 2019: Pakistan closed its airspace to overflights following major clashes with India in the Kashmir region, including airstrikes on both sides.

OPLR.name: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province (partial)
OPLR.conflictType: Insurgency (violent non-state actors) + Kashmir territorial dispute
OPLR.narrative: Covers the north-western province, where the Kashmir dispute adds a misidentification risk on top of the VNSA activity common to both restricted Pakistani provinces.

cross.detail: Tensions between Pakistan and India in the disputed Kashmir region, along with longstanding militant activity in parts of western Pakistan, create an ongoing risk in the OPKR/Karachi and OPLR/Lahore FIRs. Several states and EASA maintain altitude-based restrictions rather than full avoidance, generally advising operators to remain at or above FL260. The primary risks are from anti-aviation weaponry including the potential availability of MANPADS below FL260, and inadvertent risk from military activity or misidentification in the Kashmir region. Major events: Feb 2026: Cross-border strikes between Pakistan and Afghanistan escalated; no new airspace closures issued and commercial traffic continues to transit OAKX/Kabul FIR, including via P500 and G500. May 2025: Four days of cross-border strikes and shelling between India and Pakistan in the Kashmir region; ceasefire announced on 10 May has largely held. Some operators temporarily rerouted south via the Gulf of Oman and UAE. Jan 2024: Iran conducted missile and drone strikes against a militant group in western Pakistan, highlighting cross-border military activity risk. Dec 2023 - ongoing: Crew reports of GPS spoofing in the OPLR/Lahore FIR area, particularly around OPLA/Lahore. Feb-Aug 2019: Pakistan closed its airspace to overflights following major clashes with India in the Kashmir region, including airstrikes on both sides.

OAKX.name: FIR Kabul
OAKX.conflictType: Post-conflict security vacuum — extremist groups active, limited air traffic services
OAKX.narrative: Since the 2021 Taliban takeover, Afghanistan has had little to no functioning air traffic control. The Kabul FIR is Class G airspace: crews use published contingency routes and TIBA procedures rather than normal ATC clearances. Traffic through the FIR increased in early 2026 as flights sought a northern bypass around the closed central Middle East corridor. Some countries restrict overflights to airways P500 and G500 in the far east of the FIR; others allow overflights across the entire airspace at and above FL320.

cross.detail: March 2026: Afghanistan's airspace (OAKX/Kabul FIR) remains open but has no ATC service. The FIR is uncontrolled Class G airspace following the withdrawal of US and allied forces in Aug 2021. Overflights must be on specific contingency routes. The primary risk is from surface-to-air fire targeting aircraft at low altitudes, combined with no ATC service and an extreme threat to aircraft and crew safety on the ground. Major events: March 2026: Traffic increased through OAKX/Kabul FIR as flights used the northern bypass route around the closed Middle East corridor. Feb 2026: Cross-border strikes between Pakistan and Afghanistan escalated; commercial traffic continues to transit the FIR including via P500 and G500. Aug 2021: US and allied forces withdrew from Afghanistan; the OAKX/Kabul FIR became uncontrolled Class G airspace with no ATC service.

HAAA.name: FIR Addis Ababa, north of 8.5°N
HAAA.conflictType: Regional/border tension — assessed by EASA as medium risk
HAAA.narrative: This is an EASA Information Note, not a CZIB — meaning EASA's risk assessment group judged the risk here as medium rather than high. Full analytical detail is restricted to the CZ Hub.
HAAA.restrictionLabel: Caution only — factor into your own risk assessment and routing, below FL 260

cross.detail: The airspace risk picture in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region (the Ethiopia/Eritrea border) has been improving since a peace deal was agreed in early Nov 2022. Airspace warnings remain in place; several states advise avoiding the area. The primary risk is from large-scale ceasefire violations involving missiles or anti-aircraft weaponry that could affect overflights — civil aircraft being mistaken for military targets or caught in crossfire. Major events: Feb 2024: New flare-up in fighting in the Amhara region (south of Tigray region), including airstrikes. Nov 2022: Peace deal agreed in the Tigray region; Ethiopian Airlines planning to resume flights to HAMK/Mekele airport. Nov 2021: Several western countries issued airspace warnings and do-not-travel advisories for the Tigray region following increased fighting. July 2021: HAAA/Addis FIR published a NOTAM closing a section of airspace below FL290 over the Tigray, following reports that militia shot down a military transport near Mekele. Nov 2020: Major escalation of the conflict in the Tigray region; some airways closed by the Ethiopian and Sudanese CAAs, while others close to the conflict zone remained open. Multiple airports targeted by rockets; missiles fired into Eritrea targeting HHAS/Asmara; HABD/Bahir Dar and HAGN/Gondar also targeted. Sep 2018: Ethiopian ATC controllers went on strike; the ECAA and Ethiopian Airlines recruited retired and foreign controllers to maintain service. The strike ended Sep 7.

VYYF.name: FIR Yangon, below FL260
VYYF.conflictType: Internal armed conflict — assessed by EASA as medium risk
VYYF.narrative: As with Ethiopia, this is a medium-risk Information Note rather than a do-not-operate CZIB. France's own national guidance goes slightly further operationally, setting a hard altitude floor. GPS jamming has also been reported in the north of the FIR on overflights between China and Bangladesh airspace.
VYYF.restrictionLabel: Caution only — factor into your own risk assessment and routing, below FL 260

cross.detail: The security situation in Myanmar has deteriorated since the military coup in Feb 2021. Conflict and violence across many parts of the country involve airstrikes and armed clashes. Several countries have issued airspace warnings at the lower flight levels due to military operations, surface-to-air fire and anti-aviation weaponry. GPS jamming (and possible spoofing) has been reported in the north of the FIR on overflights between China and Bangladesh airspace. Major events: Jan 2024: Armed group shot down a military helicopter in the northern state of Kachin, likely using a MANPAD. Sep 2023: Several attacks by rebel groups against military targets nationwide, including a makeshift drone dropping bombs on aircraft hangars at an airbase next to VYNT/Naypyitaw airport. Sep 2023: Reports of intermittent GPS jamming on airway N895 over the mainland in the VYYF/Yangon FIR. Apr 2023: Myanmar's main airport VYYY/Yangon temporarily closed following an attack by resistance groups using improvised artillery rounds. Sep 2022: A Myanmar National Airlines passenger reportedly shot as bullets passed through the fuselage of an ATR 72 on approach to VYLK/Loikaw. Feb 2021: Military coup ousted the government; ATC strike at the end of Feb resulted in no ATC service for overflights. Since then, increasing strikes, mass protests, armed clashes and airstrikes on militia-active areas have continued.
